sections.heading: What Blood Pressure Checks Are
sections.bodyMarkdown:
A blood pressure check measures the force of blood against your artery walls as your heart beats and rests. The result is two numbers — systolic over diastolic — recorded in millimetres of mercury (mmHg). A pharmacy check helps identify raised readings early, when many people still feel completely well.

Participating pharmacies in England can deliver the NHS Hypertension Case-Finding Service — a free screening service for eligible adults that looks for undiagnosed high blood pressure and guides you to the right follow-up. The pharmacist measures your blood pressure using a validated device, explains your result, and arranges the next step. That may include ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) — a wearable monitor that records readings over 24 hours — or referral to your GP.

A pharmacy check screens for raised blood pressure. It does not diagnose hypertension from a single reading. Confirming a diagnosis and planning long-term treatment is your GP's role.

Some pharmacies also offer private blood pressure checks for a fee. These are separate from the NHS service — ask what is available locally and whether a charge applies.

Blood pressure checks do not replace your GP for ongoing heart health management. They give you a convenient route to screening and a clear handover when medical review is needed.

Not every pharmacy offers the NHS service or ABPM, and local participation varies — confirm before you travel.

sections.heading: Who Should Consider A Blood Pressure Check
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Routine screening if you are 40 or over** — The NHS service is aimed at adults aged 40 and above who do not already have a confirmed diagnosis of high blood pressure. Many people in this group have not had a recent check.

**Younger adults with a reason to check** — If you are under 40, you may still be offered a check at the pharmacist's discretion — for example, if you have a close family history of high blood pressure, stroke, or heart disease. Your GP can also refer patients of any age for a clinic or ambulatory check where a local arrangement exists.

**If a home reading concerned you** — A home monitor can be useful, but technique and timing affect the result. A pharmacy measurement follows a standard method and can help you understand whether follow-up is needed.

**You may not be suitable for the NHS case-finding service if:**

- You are under 40 without a recognised exception or GP referral

- You already have a diagnosis of high blood pressure and are regularly monitored by a healthcare professional

- You need blood pressure measured every day for a set period

- You have atrial fibrillation or a history of irregular heartbeat

- A correctly sized cuff is not available for your arm

If the NHS service is not suitable, the pharmacy team will tell you clearly and advise on alternatives — which may include a private check, contacting your GP, or another local service.

Pregnant women, children, and people with symptoms that suggest an emergency should not rely on a routine pharmacy screening appointment. They need assessment through the appropriate urgent or maternity pathway.

sections.heading: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Blood pressure is written as two numbers. The first (systolic) is the pressure when your heart beats. The second (diastolic) is the pressure when your heart rests between beats.

For a clinic reading in pharmacy, these bands are used to decide your next step:



| Reading | What it generally means |

| --- | --- |

| Below 90/60 | Low — may need review if you have symptoms |

| 90/60 to below 140/90 | Within the normal screening range |

| 140/90 to below 180/120 | Raised — needs further measurement before any diagnosis |

| 180/120 or higher | Very high — needs prompt medical review |



High blood pressure rarely causes obvious symptoms. That is why screening matters — a normal result is reassuring, but feeling well does not rule out a raised reading.

One reading on its own — at home, in pharmacy, or at your GP — is not enough to diagnose high blood pressure. Repeated measurement is required, and ABPM is the preferred method to confirm whether readings stay raised throughout the day.

If your reading is higher in a clinical setting than at home, you may have white-coat hypertension — where anxiety in a medical environment temporarily raises the result. ABPM or home monitoring over time helps tell the difference.

sections.heading: What Happens During The Appointment
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Contact the pharmacy to ask whether you can walk in or need to book. When you arrive, the team will confirm whether the service is suitable for you and explain what will happen.

You will be seen in a private consultation area. The pharmacist or trained pharmacy staff will ask about your health history, current medicines, and any symptoms. They will check whether you are eligible for the NHS service and explain how your result will be shared with your GP.

Before measurement, you will be asked to rest quietly for a few minutes. You should sit with your arm supported and wear loose clothing so the cuff can be placed on bare skin. Avoid caffeine for about 30 minutes beforehand if possible, and do not come straight from vigorous exercise.

The team takes your blood pressure using a validated automatic device. More than one reading may be taken — the lower of the final two is usually recorded. If readings differ significantly between arms, the arm with the higher result is used for any further checks.

Your result is explained immediately. You receive a record of your reading. Depending on the result, the next step may be a routine re-check in future years, an offer of ABPM, or referral to your GP with a recommended timeframe. A brief discussion about lifestyle factors that affect heart health — such as weight, activity, smoking, and salt intake — may form part of the consultation.

A clinic check alone usually takes around 10 to 20 minutes. If ABPM is offered, you will have a separate visit to fit the device and another to return it. The monitor typically stays on for around 24 hours during your waking hours.

Bring a list of your current medicines. Continue taking prescribed medicines as usual unless your GP has told you otherwise.

sections.heading: What Your Results May Mean
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**If your reading is within the normal range** — No further action is usually needed immediately. You will be advised when to have your blood pressure checked again — typically around every five years, or sooner if you are close to the upper limit or have other health factors such as diabetes.

**If your reading is raised** — This does not mean you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure. The pharmacy will offer ABPM where the NHS service applies, so your blood pressure can be measured across a full day rather than at a single moment. If a device is available, fitting may happen the same day or within a few days.

**After ABPM** — The average daytime reading determines the next step. You will be referred to your GP with a recommended appointment timeframe. Some results need a routine appointment within three weeks; others need review within seven days or on the same day. The pharmacy explains the urgency clearly and notifies your GP.

**If you decline ABPM** — After a raised clinic reading, you should still see your GP within three weeks for further assessment.

**If your reading is very high** — The pharmacy arranges prompt medical review. This is not a wait-and-see situation.

**If your reading is low** — A low result is only significant if you have symptoms such as dizziness, fainting, or fatigue. The pharmacist advises whether you need review and how soon.

Your GP receives your result under the NHS service. Urgent findings are sent immediately; routine results are shared through the standard local process. The pharmacy check is the start of a pathway — not the end of your care.

sections.heading: When Urgent Medical Review Is Needed
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Blood pressure screening is not for emergencies. Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, suspected stroke, severe breathing difficulty, collapse, sudden confusion, or any life-threatening symptom — regardless of what a blood pressure reading shows.

**Seek same-day medical review** if your clinic reading is 180/120 or higher (even without symptoms), if ABPM shows a very high average, if the device detects an irregular pulse that is not already known and investigated, or if your reading is low and you experience regular fainting, falls, or daily fear of fainting.

**Call 999 immediately** if a very high reading is accompanied by chest pain, severe headache with neurological symptoms, new confusion, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney problems.

The NHS pharmacy service is not appropriate when you need emergency care, when you require daily blood pressure monitoring over a set period, when you are pregnant and need maternity blood pressure assessment, or when you fall outside the service eligibility criteria without a GP referral.

If the service is not suitable, the pharmacy team tells you where to go next. You should never leave without a clear plan.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Do I need an appointment or can I walk in?**
Some pharmacies offer walk-in checks; others prefer you to book so a consultation room and staff time can be set aside. Call ahead to ask what your pharmacy offers and whether same-day help is available.

**I am under 40 but my parent had high blood pressure — can I still get checked?**
You may be offered a check at the pharmacist's discretion if you have a recognised family history. Ask when you call. If the NHS service is not suitable, a private check or GP appointment may be the better route.

**What if I am not eligible for the NHS service?**
The team explains why and tells you what to do instead — which may include contacting your GP, booking a private check, or using another local service. You should leave with a clear next step.

**Will one high reading mean I have high blood pressure?**
No. A single raised reading — at home or in pharmacy — is not a diagnosis. Further measurement over time, usually with ABPM, is needed before your GP can confirm whether you have high blood pressure.

**What is ABPM and why might I need it?**
ABPM is offered when a clinic reading is raised but not in the emergency range — because a single pharmacy reading can be affected by nerves, recent activity, or timing. The monitor records across your normal day so your GP can see whether blood pressure stays raised or was a one-off elevation.

**Can the pharmacy start or change my blood pressure medication?**
No. Long-term blood pressure treatment is managed by your GP. The pharmacy role is screening, monitoring where the service allows, and referral.

**My home monitor shows a different result — which should I trust?**
Home monitors can be helpful but must be used correctly — right cuff size, rested arm, consistent timing. Bring your readings to the appointment. The pharmacy follows a standard clinical method; your GP interprets the overall pattern.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
publishDefault: false

**Myth: One high reading means I have hypertension.**
Reality: Diagnosis requires confirmed repeated measurements and GP assessment — not a single clinic or home reading.

**Myth: High blood pressure always causes symptoms.**
Reality: Many people with raised blood pressure feel completely well. That is why screening exists.

**Myth: The pharmacy will put me on blood pressure tablets.**
Reality: Pharmacists screen and refer. Starting or adjusting long-term treatment is your GP's role.

**Myth: Every pharmacy blood pressure check is a free NHS service.**
Reality: The NHS Hypertension Case-Finding Service is offered only at participating pharmacies. Private checks may carry a fee.

**Myth: If I feel fine, I do not need a check.**
Reality: High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Risk factors and age — not how you feel — determine whether screening is sensible.

**Myth: Home monitors replace professional checks.**
Reality: Home monitoring supports ongoing awareness, but validated clinical measurement and GP review remain important for diagnosis and treatment decisions.

sections.heading: Patient Concerns
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Concern: A high result means I will be forced onto medication immediately.**

A raised reading starts a assessment pathway — not automatic treatment. Your GP considers your overall cardiovascular risk, lifestyle, and confirmed readings before recommending any medicine. Lifestyle changes are often part of the plan.

**Concern: I will be judged for smoking, weight, or drinking.**

Lifestyle questions help the pharmacist give relevant advice and signpost support services. Consultations are private and professional — the aim is to help, not to criticise.

**Concern: Anxiety will make my reading wrong, so the result is useless.**

Feeling nervous can temporarily raise a reading. That is a recognised pattern. ABPM exists partly to see what happens outside a clinical setting. Tell the pharmacist if you are anxious — it helps them interpret the result.

sections.heading: Why Patients Choose Blood Pressure Checks
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Patients choose pharmacy blood pressure checks because they offer convenient access to screening without waiting for a routine GP appointment. For many people, a local visit fits around work and family commitments more easily than a surgery appointment.

The service gives a clear outcome in one visit: a explained result, a record for your own files, and a defined next step. Where the NHS service applies, eligible patients pay nothing for the screening itself.

Early detection matters because untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke, heart disease, and kidney problems over time — often without warning symptoms.

sections.heading: Why Patients Choose A Community Pharmacy
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Medicines expertise** — Pharmacists understand how prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect blood pressure. That knowledge informs the questions they ask during your check.

**Accessible location** — Community pharmacies are on high streets and in neighbourhoods. Many open beyond standard GP hours, including evenings and weekends.

**Continuity** — If you already collect prescriptions from the same pharmacy, the team may already know your medicines history, which supports a more informed conversation.

**Face-to-face support** — You speak to a qualified professional in a private setting, ask questions in your own words, and leave knowing what happens next.

sections.heading: Trust And Safety
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Pharmacists are degree-qualified healthcare professionals with a legal duty to put patient safety first.

The NHS Hypertension Case-Finding Service follows written national clinical rules that define who can be screened, how measurements are taken, when ABPM is offered, and when GP referral is required. These are structured safety processes — not informal judgements.

If a reading or symptom falls outside what pharmacy screening can safely manage, the team will not treat it as a routine check. They refer you through the appropriate pathway — same-day GP review, urgent care, or emergency services. That honest signposting is how the service protects you.

sections.heading: Booking And Next Steps
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Call {{phone}} to confirm whether this pharmacy offers the NHS blood pressure check service or private screening, and whether you need an appointment. Ask about ABPM availability if you think you may need it.

Opening hours: {{opening_hours}}

Book online: {{booking_link}}

Before you attend, note your current medicines, any recent home readings, and whether you have a family history of high blood pressure or heart disease. Wear loose sleeves and avoid caffeine for about 30 minutes beforehand if possible.

Consultations take place in a {{consultation_room}}. NHS service availability: {{nhs_service}}. Private checks: {{private_service}}.

After your check, follow the advice you are given — whether that is returning for ABPM, booking a GP appointment within the timeframe explained, or scheduling your next routine screening. If you develop urgent symptoms at any point, seek emergency help. Do not wait for a follow-up appointment if you feel seriously unwell.

A pharmacy blood pressure check is one step in looking after your heart health. Used appropriately, it helps you find raised readings early, understand what they mean, and reach your GP when medical review is needed.

Call {{phone}} to book or ask about walk-in availability.

Some pharmacies offer walk-in checks; others prefer you to book so a consultation room and staff time can be set aside. Call ahead to ask what your pharmacy offers and whether same-day help is available.

**I am under 40 but my parent had high blood pressure — can I still get checked?**
You may be offered a check at the pharmacist's discretion if you have a recognised family history. Ask when you call. If the NHS service is not suitable, a private check or GP appointment may be the better route.

**What if I am not eligible for the NHS service?**
The team explains why and tells you what to do instead — which may include contacting your GP, booking a private check, or using another local service. You should leave with a clear next step.

**Will one high reading mean I have high blood pressure?**
No. A single raised reading — at home or in pharmacy — is not a diagnosis. Further measurement over time, usually with ABPM, is needed before your GP can confirm whether you have high blood pressure.

**What is ABPM and why might I need it?**
ABPM is offered when a clinic reading is raised but not in the emergency range — because a single pharmacy reading can be affected by nerves, recent activity, or timing. The monitor records across your normal day so your GP can see whether blood pressure stays raised or was a one-off elevation.

**Can the pharmacy start or change my blood pressure medication?**
No. Long-term blood pressure treatment is managed by your GP. The pharmacy role is screening, monitoring where the service allows, and referral.

**My home monitor shows a different result — which should I trust?**
Home monitors can be helpful but must be used correctly — right cuff size, rested arm, consistent timing. Bring your readings to the appointment. The pharmacy follows a standard clinical method; your GP interprets the overall pattern.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions
sections.bodyMarkdown:
publishDefault: false

**Myth: One high reading means I have hypertension.**
Reality: Diagnosis requires confirmed repeated measurements and GP assessment — not a single clinic or home reading.

**Myth: High blood pressure always causes symptoms.**
Reality: Many people with raised blood pressure feel completely well. That is why screening exists.

**Myth: The pharmacy will put me on blood pressure tablets.**
Reality: Pharmacists screen and refer. Starting or adjusting long-term treatment is your GP's role.

**Myth: Every pharmacy blood pressure check is a free NHS service.**
Reality: The NHS Hypertension Case-Finding Service is offered only at participating pharmacies. Private checks may carry a fee.

**Myth: If I feel fine, I do not need a check.**
Reality: High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Risk factors and age — not how you feel — determine whether screening is sensible.

**Myth: Home monitors replace professional checks.**
Reality: Home monitoring supports ongoing awareness, but validated clinical measurement and GP review remain important for diagnosis and treatment decisions.

sections.heading: Patient Concerns
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Concern: A high result means I will be forced onto medication immediately.**

A raised reading starts a assessment pathway — not automatic treatment. Your GP considers your overall cardiovascular risk, lifestyle, and confirmed readings before recommending any medicine. Lifestyle changes are often part of the plan.

**Concern: I will be judged for smoking, weight, or drinking.**

Lifestyle questions help the pharmacist give relevant advice and signpost support services. Consultations are private and professional — the aim is to help, not to criticise.

**Concern: Anxiety will make my reading wrong, so the result is useless.**

Feeling nervous can temporarily raise a reading. That is a recognised pattern. ABPM exists partly to see what happens outside a clinical setting. Tell the pharmacist if you are anxious — it helps them interpret the result.

sections.heading: Why Patients Choose Blood Pressure Checks
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Patients choose pharmacy blood pressure checks because they offer convenient access to screening without waiting for a routine GP appointment. For many people, a local visit fits around work and family commitments more easily than a surgery appointment.

The service gives a clear outcome in one visit: a explained result, a record for your own files, and a defined next step. Where the NHS service applies, eligible patients pay nothing for the screening itself.

Early detection matters because untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke, heart disease, and kidney problems over time — often without warning symptoms.

sections.heading: Why Patients Choose A Community Pharmacy
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Medicines expertise** — Pharmacists understand how prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect blood pressure. That knowledge informs the questions they ask during your check.

**Accessible location** — Community pharmacies are on high streets and in neighbourhoods. Many open beyond standard GP hours, including evenings and weekends.

**Continuity** — If you already collect prescriptions from the same pharmacy, the team may already know your medicines history, which supports a more informed conversation.

**Face-to-face support** — You speak to a qualified professional in a private setting, ask questions in your own words, and leave knowing what happens next.

sections.heading: Trust And Safety
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Pharmacists are degree-qualified healthcare professionals with a legal duty to put patient safety first.

The NHS Hypertension Case-Finding Service follows written national clinical rules that define who can be screened, how measurements are taken, when ABPM is offered, and when GP referral is required. These are structured safety processes — not informal judgements.

If a reading or symptom falls outside what pharmacy screening can safely manage, the team will not treat it as a routine check. They refer you through the appropriate pathway — same-day GP review, urgent care, or emergency services. That honest signposting is how the service protects you.

sections.heading: Booking And Next Steps
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Call {{phone}} to confirm whether this pharmacy offers the NHS blood pressure check service or private screening, and whether you need an appointment. Ask about ABPM availability if you think you may need it.

Opening hours: {{opening_hours}}

Book online: {{booking_link}}

Before you attend, note your current medicines, any recent home readings, and whether you have a family history of high blood pressure or heart disease. Wear loose sleeves and avoid caffeine for about 30 minutes beforehand if possible.

Consultations take place in a {{consultation_room}}. NHS service availability: {{nhs_service}}. Private checks: {{private_service}}.

After your check, follow the advice you are given — whether that is returning for ABPM, booking a GP appointment within the timeframe explained, or scheduling your next routine screening. If you develop urgent symptoms at any point, seek emergency help. Do not wait for a follow-up appointment if you feel seriously unwell.

A pharmacy blood pressure check is one step in looking after your heart health. Used appropriately, it helps you find raised readings early, understand what they mean, and reach your GP when medical review is needed.

intro.body: Pharmacy blood pressure checks offer convenient screening between GP reviews — with clear advice on whether follow-up is needed.
Regular blood pressure monitoring helps identify raised readings early, when lifestyle changes or GP review may be most useful.
A pharmacy check measures your blood pressure, explains the result in plain language, and guides appropriate next steps.
Many people choose pharmacy screening because it fits around everyday commitments without waiting for a routine GP slot.
Blood pressure checks at a community pharmacy complement GP care — screening, advice and referral when clinically appropriate.

problem.heading: Why Blood Pressure Matters
problem.body: High blood pressure often has no symptoms but can increase stroke, heart disease and kidney risk over time. Risk factors such as age over 40, family history, diabetes and lifestyle habits influence how often screening is useful.
bullets: Do I need to see a GP?

problem.heading: Understanding Hypertension Risk
problem.body: Hypertension frequently causes no obvious warning signs, which is why routine measurement matters. Cardiovascular risk rises when readings stay elevated — early detection supports timely GP follow-up.

problem.heading: When Screening Helps
problem.body: Screening is especially valuable for adults over 40, those with family history of hypertension, and people managing diabetes or high cardiovascular risk. One reading does not diagnose hypertension.

problem.heading: Cardiovascular Health Basics
problem.body: Blood pressure reflects how hard the heart and vessels work. Sustained high readings warrant further assessment — pharmacy checks identify raised readings and guide proportionate follow-up.

problem.heading: Why Regular Checks Matter
problem.body: Untreated hypertension increases long-term harm even without symptoms. Pharmacy screening supports the NHS Hypertension Case-Finding pathway where commissioned — with referral to GP when needed.

benefits.heading: Benefits Of Pharmacy Screening
benefits.body: Community pharmacy checks offer accessible measurement, lifestyle advice and clear signposting without always needing a GP appointment first.

benefits.heading: What The Service Delivers
benefits.body: You receive a professional measurement, discussion of risk factors, and guidance on whether repeat checks or GP review is advisable.

benefits.heading: Practical Advantages
benefits.body: Pharmacy-led checks fit around work and family routines. Results are explained before you leave — with safety-netting if symptoms require urgent care.

benefits.heading: Patient-Focused Support
benefits.body: The service focuses on screening and education — helping you understand readings and when GP involvement is clinically appropriate.

benefits.heading: Accessible Heart Health Checks
benefits.body: Screening in a community setting lowers barriers for people who delay GP contact. Pharmacists explain results and next steps clearly.

eligibility.heading: Who Should Have A Check
eligibility.body: Suitability is confirmed individually. Adults over 40, those with risk factors, or people due a routine review may benefit — but diagnosis requires GP assessment, not one pharmacy reading alone.

eligibility.heading: Who The Service Suits
eligibility.body: The check suits people seeking screening, monitoring between GP reviews, or advice after home readings. Emergency symptoms such as chest pain need urgent care, not a pharmacy check alone.

eligibility.heading: Eligibility Overview
eligibility.body: Individual assessment confirms whether a pharmacy check is appropriate. Some NHS pathways have commissioning criteria — availability and eligibility are confirmed at booking.

eligibility.heading: Before You Book
eligibility.body: Share relevant medical history and medicines at assessment. The pharmacist confirms scope — and signposts to GP or urgent care when symptoms fall outside pharmacy screening.

eligibility.heading: Is This Right For Me
eligibility.body: If you are unsure whether pharmacy screening suits your situation, contact the pharmacy team. Complex or symptomatic cases may need GP review first.

howItWorks.heading: How The Check Works
howItWorks.body: The appointment covers measurement, lifestyle discussion and referral advice. Each step is explained — with GP signposting when results or symptoms require it.

howItWorks.heading: Your Appointment Steps
howItWorks.body: You rest briefly, then receive a cuff measurement. The pharmacist discusses readings, risk factors and whether repeat checks or GP follow-up is advisable.

howItWorks.heading: The Screening Process
howItWorks.body: Screening follows a structured pathway: preparation, measurement, interpretation and safety-netting. Diagnosis and long-term treatment remain with your GP.

howItWorks.heading: What Happens During The Check
howItWorks.body: A pharmacist measures blood pressure, reviews context such as age and risk factors, and explains whether your reading suggests further action.

howItWorks.heading: Measurement And Follow-Up
howItWorks.body: After measurement, you receive plain-language interpretation. Raised readings may prompt repeat checks, home monitoring advice, or GP referral under NHS pathways.

preparationGuide.heading: Preparing For Your Check
preparationGuide.body: Preparation improves accuracy. Rest before measurement, wear loose sleeves, and bring previous home readings if you monitor.

preparationGuide.heading: Before Your Appointment
preparationGuide.body: Avoid strenuous exercise and heavy meals immediately beforehand. Note any symptoms, medicines and recent home readings to discuss.

preparationGuide.heading: What To Bring
preparationGuide.body: Bring previous readings, a medicines list, and any GP correspondence about hypertension. This helps the pharmacist give proportionate advice.

preparationGuide.heading: Getting Accurate Results
preparationGuide.body: Sit quietly for several minutes before measurement. Empty bladder if needed, and keep arm supported at heart level during the reading.

preparationGuide.heading: Appointment Preparation
preparationGuide.body: Allow time for discussion after measurement. If you smoke or drink caffeine, mention timing — both can temporarily affect readings.

trustSafety.heading: Safety And Professional Standards
trustSafety.body: Pharmacy checks screen for raised readings — they do not diagnose or treat hypertension on the spot. Diagnosis and long-term management remain with your GP.

trustSafety.heading: When To Seek GP Or Urgent Care
trustSafety.body: Chest pain, severe headache, sudden vision changes or neurological symptoms require urgent medical attention — not a routine pharmacy check alone.

trustSafety.heading: Professional Insight
trustSafety.body: Pharmacist-led screening works best when patients understand limits of a single reading and follow advice on repeat measurement or GP review.

trustSafety.heading: Trust And Clinical Governance
trustSafety.body: Regulated pharmacy teams follow clinical governance for NHS screening pathways where commissioned, with clear scope and referral criteria.

patientEducation.heading: Understanding Your Reading
patientEducation.body: Blood pressure is recorded as systolic over diastolic (mmHg). One raised check warrants follow-up — not immediate diagnosis.

patientEducation.heading: Patient Education
patientEducation.body: Educational guidance covers what happens during screening, NHS pathway eligibility, and when GP or urgent care is more appropriate.

patientEducation.heading: Learning About Blood Pressure
patientEducation.body: Understanding risk factors — salt, weight, activity, alcohol and smoking — helps you act on pharmacist lifestyle advice between reviews.

patientEducation.heading: What To Expect After Screening
patientEducation.body: You may be advised to monitor at home, repeat the check, or see your GP. Written summary helps you track next steps.

mythVsFact.heading: Myths Vs Facts
mythVsFact.body: Evidence-based pharmacy advice separates common misconceptions from accurate information:
bullets: Myth: A pharmacy diagnoses hypertension on the spot. Fact: Screening identifies raised readings — diagnosis and treatment remain with your GP.
Myth: High blood pressure always causes symptoms. Fact: Hypertension is often silent — screening matters.
Myth: One normal reading means no future checks needed. Fact: Risk factors determine how often you should be monitored.

mythVsFact.heading: Common Misconceptions
mythVsFact.body: Clear facts help you make informed decisions about screening and follow-up:
bullets: Myth: Pharmacy replaces your GP. Fact: Pharmacy services complement GP care.
Myth: Every check is free for everyone. Fact: NHS eligibility varies by pathway and location.
Myth: Home monitors replace professional checks. Fact: Both have roles — discuss readings with a clinician.

mythVsFact.heading: Facts About Pharmacy Screening
mythVsFact.body: Separating myths from facts supports safe use of community screening:
bullets: Myth: Caffeine does not affect readings. Fact: It can — rest before measurement.
Myth: Only older adults need checks. Fact: Risk factors matter at any adult age.
Myth: Treatment starts in pharmacy. Fact: GPs manage long-term hypertension treatment.

mythVsFact.heading: Hypertension Myths Clarified
mythVsFact.body: Accurate information improves heart health decisions:
bullets: Myth: Stress readings are always wrong. Fact: Repeat measurement and ABPM may be needed.
Myth: All pharmacies offer identical NHS services. Fact: Commissioning varies.
Myth: Lifestyle changes never help. Fact: They are often first-line alongside medical review.

faqs.question: Do I need an appointment for a blood pressure check?
faqs.answer: Booking ahead is recommended so adequate time is allowed for measurement and discussion — typically 10–20 minutes.

faqs.question: How long does a blood pressure appointment take?
faqs.answer: Most consultations take 10–20 minutes including measurement, lifestyle advice and follow-up planning.

faqs.question: Can a pharmacy diagnose high blood pressure?
faqs.answer: No — pharmacy checks screen for raised readings. Diagnosis and long-term treatment remain with your GP.

faqs.question: How often should I have my blood pressure checked?
faqs.answer: Frequency depends on age, risk factors and previous readings. Over-40s and those with risk factors benefit from regular checks.

faqs.question: Is a pharmacy blood pressure check free?
faqs.answer: NHS Hypertension Case-Finding may be free where commissioned. Private checks may incur a fee — confirm at booking.

faqs.question: What should I do before my check?
faqs.answer: Rest for five minutes, wear loose sleeves, avoid caffeine for 30 minutes if possible, and bring any home readings.

faqs.question: What if my reading is high?
faqs.answer: Raised readings may prompt repeat measurement, home monitoring advice, or GP referral — depending on context and NHS pathway criteria.

faqs.question: Can I walk in without booking?
faqs.answer: Walk-in availability varies. Booking ensures dedicated time for accurate measurement and advice.

faqs.question: What do systolic and diastolic numbers mean?
faqs.answer: Systolic is pressure when the heart beats; diastolic is when it rests — both are recorded in mmHg.

faqs.question: Should I bring my medicines list?
faqs.answer: Yes — some medicines affect blood pressure. Sharing your list helps the pharmacist give accurate advice.

faqs.question: When should I see a GP instead?
faqs.answer: Ongoing treatment, diagnosis, or symptoms such as chest pain require GP or urgent care — not screening alone.

faqs.question: What is ambulatory blood pressure monitoring?
faqs.answer: ABPM records readings over 24 hours and may be recommended when clinic readings are borderline or inconsistent.

faqs.question: Can lifestyle changes lower blood pressure?
faqs.answer: Weight management, salt reduction, activity and alcohol moderation can help — discuss a plan with your GP or pharmacist.

faqs.question: Are home monitors reliable?
faqs.answer: Validated home monitors can be useful when used correctly. Bring readings to discuss with a pharmacist or GP.

faqs.question: What symptoms need urgent care?
faqs.answer: Chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe headache or sudden vision changes need urgent medical attention.
